## What this file checks

Rendering this document exercises the Python half of the toolchain. Quarto has to
find this project's Python, start a Jupyter kernel in it, run the code below, and
hand the result to a typesetter.

R is checked by `check-quarto-r.qmd` rather than here. Keeping one language per
document means neither needs `reticulate`, which would otherwise have to locate
this project's Python from inside R -- a thing that goes wrong often enough that
it is not worth meeting in week one.

If you get a PDF and an HTML file, all of those pieces work.

## Python and pandas

```{python}
import sys
import pandas as pd

print(sys.version)
print("pandas", pd.__version__)
```

```{python}
pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "course": ["DSCI 511", "DSCI 521", "DSCI 523"],
        "block": [1, 1, 2],
        "language": ["Python", "Python", "R"],
    }
)
```

## Characters that are not plain English

Assignments regularly contain accents, Greek letters, degree signs, proper dashes
and emoji. Not every output route can typeset all of them, and that is expected
rather than a fault in your installation:

Montréal · naïve · Öl · 5 °C · α β γ · 10 – 20 · "curly quotes" · ✅ ❌ 📊 ⚠️

Mathematics is typeset separately from ordinary text, so it works everywhere:
$\alpha = 0.05$ and $\hat{\beta} = (X^{\top}X)^{-1}X^{\top}y$.

**What you should see.** In the HTML and in the Typst PDF, every character above
appears. In the LaTeX PDF the accents, the dashes and the mathematics appear, but
the Greek letters and the emoji do not — LaTeX has no glyph for them and drops
them silently. If an assignment needs emoji in a PDF, render it with Typst.
